Now other nations are looking for radical security solutions iNews 15th July 2026 , Kieron Monks Foreign news and feature writer As wars and predator states reshape the world order, fears are growing that a new nuclear arms race is already under way. Agreements between the great powers over the control of nuclear weapons are breaking down. Middle powers, from South Korea to Saudi Arabia, are considering radical solutions to their security concerns. The Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), which binds 190 countries to the status quo of restricting nuclear weapons to the handful of states that already possess them, has largely held for a generation. North Korea is the only new nuclear power of the 21st century. Dr Pavel Podvig, a senior researcher into weapons of mass destruction at the UN Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR), noted a rise in “magic wand thinking”, with several governments openly discussing nuclear development. “There is this idea that nuclear weapons just work automatically to protect you, when the reality is more complicated,” he said. John Erath, senior policy director at the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation in Washington DC, said factors such as Russia’s nuclear threats and China’s expanding nuclear arsenal made this a more dangerous era for proliferation control. While he did not expect a country to cross the threshold in the near future, one new nuclear nation could trigger a flood. “If Iran were to build a nuclear weapon, I believe several other countries would as well,” he said. Here are the countries that are among those most likely to join the ranks of nuclear powers… South Korea Seoul has lived under threat from its nuclear northern neighbour for decades within a still-unresolved frozen conflict that dates back to 1950. In 2023, the then president Yoon Suk-yeol – now mired in legal trouble over a failed coup – warned that South Korea could rapidly develop its own nuclear weapons if Pyongyang’s threats became “more serious” – a position that reflected public opinion and the country’s capabilities. Taehwa Hong, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the country was a “plausible candidate” to join the nuclear club, more so for the US downsizing its military presence there. “The drivers are real,” said Hong, who is working on a book about South Korean strategy. “Public support for an independent arsenal has run at 70 to 80 per cent for over a decade, Korea has a world-class civil nuclear industry, and confidence in US extended deterrence has been eroding under America First pressures.” “But the restraints are equally real. Weaponisation would require NPT withdrawal, expose one of the world’s most trade-dependent economies to sanctions, strain the very alliance it is meant to compensate for, and risk a proliferation cascade running through Japan.” The most likely scenario is for Seoul to approach the nuclear threshold through peaceful enrichment of nuclear fuel without crossing it, the analyst said. But that could change if the US withdraws more forces or its “nuclear umbrella” from the country, or in a scenario of China attacking Taiwan Poland Poland’s President, Karol Nawrocki, said in February that he would support the development of an independent nuclear deterrent. “The path toward a Polish nuclear project, in full respect of all international regulations, is a path Poland should pursue,” he said. Those sentiments were echoed by the liberal Prime Minister, Donald Tusk – usually a fierce opponent of Nawrocki. Polls have shown a majority of public opinion supports Poland having its own nuclear weapons outside the US umbrella. Dr Jakub Bordio, a professor of political science at the University of Wroclaw, said these were unprecedented developments driven by a sense that the “international security architecture is developing, from our perspective, in the wrong direction”. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Mark Carney and Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrive in Calgary, Alberta, to sign agreements on Thursday. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock Canada Canada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits Canadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian community Agence France-Presse Thu 10 Sep 2026 16.35 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 16.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy . Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage. “Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy. The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”. That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy. “Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation. In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent. “Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine ,” Carney said. The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program. Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks. Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply. The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals. Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures. Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine. Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.” Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period. But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war. “But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said. “And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.” After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government. He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario. Teymouri did not specify the origin of the strike.Qeshm is the largest island in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint that has been at the centre of tensions between Washington and Tehran since late February.The UKMTO maritime agency on Sunday said it had received a report that a vessel had been struck by an "unknown projectile" while transiting the Strait.It later reported that a fire had broken out onboard the ship and that local authorities were helping evacuate the crew."Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO whilst authorities are investigating," the agency added.

Photograph: Ken Wolter/Alamy US crime Minnesota professor linked to series of bizarre incidents involving urine at university Investigators determined professor responsible for urine found on a backpack, in trash cans and in water bottles Keely Aouga and Ramon Antonio Vargas Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former professor at Macalester College in the Minnesota city of St Paul is facing a felony charge for allegedly spilling his urine on a student’s backpack while he still worked at the school, costing more than $2,000 in damages, according to a state criminal court document. Paul Fischer, 55, is at the center of the bizarre, alleged workplace misconduct case that led to his being cited for first-degree damage to property – and linked to at least a half dozen such incidents involving urine at the liberal arts college over the course of a year. St Paul police homed in on Fischer after a student reported that she left her belongings unattended for about six minutes on 5 December in a common area near his office. Fischer was a biology professor at the time. The student told police that she found urine on her backpack when she returned to her belongings, according to the criminal court document obtained by the Guardian. The student reported the matter in February to St Paul police. Police learned that the college by then had also investigated her complaint – and determined there had been at least six such episodes involving urine at the school’s Olin-Rice science center during the span of about a year. Urination had been found in trash cans, individuals’ water bottles and inside professors’ decorations, the state criminal court document said. Investigators determined Fischer was responsible for the series of urine-related cases, and he resigned from Macalester College, where he had spent 25 years working. Authorities confronted Fischer before charging him, the court document said. He allegedly shared that “during the last one and a half to two years he developed a habit of urinating in a cup and disposing the contents in either trash cans or lab sinks around campus”, according to the document. The former professor allegedly claimed that he was emptying a container of urine into a trash can near his office on the day that the student who reported him said her backpack had been damaged. He said he believed that the cup of urine spilled on to the student’s belongings, the court document alleged. The urine on the student’s backpack resulted in damage to both the bag and her belongings inside, the document added. The student provided investigators with an itemized receipt for what was damaged that amounted to $2,070. Prosecutors for Ramsey county, Minnesota , whose jurisdiction includes St Paul, charged Fischer through a criminal complaint on 7 October. He could get up to five years in prison as well as a maximum fine of $10,000 if convicted as charged. A spokesperson for Macalester College on Tuesday said the school “is aware of the criminal charge against Paul Fischer” – and that his employment there ended during the 2025-2026 academic year. “As this is an ongoing legal matter involving a former employee, the college has no further comment,” the spokesperson said. Attempts to contact Fischer on Tuesday were not immediately successful. Commentary about the criminal complaint against Fischer made its way over to a page under his name on the RateMyProfessors.com platform. “So that explains the yellowish stain that appeared on my lab coat,” a comment posted on Tuesday read. The comment, which the Guardian could not authenticate, also said: “I don’t understand what motivates someone to do something like this, but avoid him at all costs.” Explore more on these topics US crime Minnesota US universities news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza , both could have played a role in Ra'am's result. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video https://p.dw.com/p/5OaeD Skip next section Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters 10/27/2026 October 27, 2026 Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters Mark Hallam Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continued issuing appeals to supporters to go out and vote online as the day progressed. One common theme was apparent in almost all of the posts: warnings about high turnout in Arab and to a lesser extent left-leaning communities. "We're at war for our home," one of Netanyahu's posts read, using a phrase that appeared repeatedly in his messaging. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!!" In another post he showed an image claiming to show a long line of voters queueing in Rahat, with a crowd of women wearing niqab coverings prominently visible at the front of the queue, suggesting that they were Muslim Palestinian voters. Sami Abou Shahadeh, the leader of the Balad party, which is part of the alliance known as the Joint List, in turn called on his supporters to vote before the deadline expired, also highlighting similar appeals to voters from the leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, Itamar Ben-Gvir. "There is one response to the incitement by Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu against the Arab citizens that has been going on all day: go out and vote for the Joint List!" he wrote. https://p.dw.com/p/5OkR4 Skip next section President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel' 10/27/2026 October 27, 2026 President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel' Mark Hallam The president of the German-Israeli Society, Green party politician Volker Beck, said in a TV interview on election day that he believed a change in leadership might be in Israel's interests. "It would be good for Israel, if it were to come to a change, because I believe that [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has squandered a great deal of trust in recent years, both in foreign and domestic policy," Beck said in an interview broadcast on sister channels RTL and ntv. Beck, a Bundestag lawmaker for more than two decades with the Greens who was perhaps best known as a politician as a campaigner for LGBT rights and advocate of an uncompromising Israeli foreign policy, is not typically associated with stern criticism of Netanyahu or his government. "Although he has also done some things right and has done some necessary things, a change is really needed" to allow Israel to recoup support among the international community, Beck said, as Netanyahu becomes an increasingly polarizing figure on the world stage. He also criticized domestic efforts by the Likud-led government to reform the legal system and its influence over politics, saying this would "fundamentally change Israel's character, and should be stopped." Beck said he hoped that a functioning majority would emerge from the vote, but acknowledged that pollsters anticipated a stalemate. In that scenario, he said, he would personally favor a national unity government incorporating all the major players. But at present he thought the "divide between the two camps is so deep, that it really would be a bit of a masterstroke to be able to bring them together." He made a similar comment online, saying such a unity govermment "would be good" but was "not very likely." https://p.dw.com/p/5OkD9 Skip next section Likud says online that it has requested an extension of voting hours 10/27/2026 October 27, 2026 Likud says online that it has requested an extension of voting hours Mark Hallam Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's Likud party wrote on the Telegram social media channel that it has submitted a request for polling stations to stay open later. "Likud: We have submitted a request to extend the voting hours!" the post said. It offered no further details, for instance, how long an extension it was seeking or whether it was to be nationwide or at individual polling stations. The Ultra-Orthodox Shas party also joined the petition, according to the Times of Israel , saying: "The parties are trying to prevent a situation in which citizens waiting in line won’t be able to vote." The main opposition Yashar party rejected the extension, saying: "No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify granting this request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for allegations challenging the integrity of the election, continuing the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning." Politicians of all stripes have been trying hard to mobilize voters for what's expected to be a tight race. Turnout has also been high so far, with long lines at some polling stations as a result of this. Voting was already set to continue quite late into the night, with polling stations scheduled to close at 10 p.m. local time. Voters who are in line at polling stations at closing time will still be allowed to vote. https://p.dw.com/p/5OkOB Skip next section Who are Israel's first-time voters projected to support? 10/27/2026 October 27, 2026 Who are Israel's first-time voters projected to support? Polls show Israel's many young voters are more likely to vote for far-right parties, particularly Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party. An opinion poll by Agam Labs at Jerusalem's Hebrew University predicts that supporters of Otzma Yehudit are younger than the average Israeli voter, with as many as a third voting for the first time. According to local media, no injuries were reported among the crew members, said Adrian Mihalcioiu, chairman of Romania's Free Seafarers' Union. The vessel, identified as the YARA J, was reportedly hit about 8 to 10 nautical miles southeast of the port of Sulina. It has a 17-member crew consisting of nationals from Syria, India and Iran. Romania's Minister of National Defense Radu Miruta said checks are being carried out to determine whether the ship was indeed struck by a drone.
